name: Phantom decoy effect
statement: An option that beats another option and is then declared unavailable is supposed to pull choices towards the option it beat.
meaning: Three alternatives, two attributes. The target and the competitor each win on one attribute, so choosing between them takes a trade-off. The phantom beats the target on both attributes and beats the competitor on only one, and it cannot be chosen. That inversion is what separates it from the decoy of the attraction effect, which sits below the target and is available. Pettibone and Wedell set the puzzle out plainly: a phantom both asymmetrically dominates the target and stretches the range upward on the target's best attribute, and both features should push choice away from the target rather than towards it. The reported finding runs the other way. Retailers know the shape of it as bait and switch, in which the advertised bargain has run out and the shopper takes its nearest neighbour.

origin.who: Anthony R. Pratkanis and Peter H. Farquhar
origin.note: The paper is a review rather than an experiment. Its abstract says the term phantom is of recent vintage, that psychological reactions to unavailable alternatives had been studied for almost 60 years, and that the paper reviews 13 domains of research to identify seven empirical generalisations about phantoms. The seven are not listed in the abstract, and the full text could not be retrieved for this entry. Pettibone and Wedell credit this paper with introducing the phantom decoy. Farquhar and Pratkanis made the applied case a year later in Management Science, arguing that phantoms should be handled openly in decision structuring because they can produce bias, deception and suboptimal decisions.

evidence: The fullest test varies where the phantom sits. Pettibone and Wedell gave 439 undergraduates 20 consumer choice sets, with each of five conditions using a different phantom position. Every set appeared for three seconds, after which one alternative was declared unavailable and its label blinked. The measure is the share choosing the target when the phantom favours it, minus the share when the phantom favours its rival. A phantom placed above the target on the target's better attribute gave 0.20, 95% interval 0.12 to 0.26. Moving that phantom further out on the same attribute gave 0.14, 0.08 to 0.20. Two positions that also lifted the target's weaker attribute gave 0.09 and 0.10. A phantom that matched the target's better attribute and lifted only its weaker one gave 0.04 and was not significant. Position mattered, F(4, 434) = 2.56, p < 0.05. Experiment 2 put all five positions inside subjects, with 262 students choosing among products described by price and a quality rating. The same two positions worked, at 0.10 and 0.05, and the other three did not. Averaged over positions the shift was about 4 points, against about 11 points in the between-subjects design. Trueblood and Pettibone report that in Pettibone and Wedell's 2000 consumer experiment the target was chosen 57% of the time when a phantom targeted it and 43% when it did not, and those two figures are quoted here from that later paper. Scarpi ran the design on cats: close phantoms shifted them towards the available food more similar to the phantom, and distant phantoms did nothing.

replication.headline: Direction depends on the materials and on when the shopper learns the option is gone. Pettibone and Wedell moved choice towards the target at four of five phantom positions, at 0.20 of a choice share at best. Trueblood and Pettibone, using rectangles instead of products, moved it towards the competitor.
replication.detail: Pettibone and Wedell's two experiments are the largest direct test located, and the shifts are small: 0.20 of a choice share at the best of five positions in Experiment 1, and 0.10 in Experiment 2. Trueblood and Pettibone ran the same five positions on a perceptual task, asking people to pick the largest of three rectangles after one was withdrawn. With 84 participants told of the withdrawal after a two-second delay, group preference ran towards the competitor, 95% highest density interval 0.453 to 0.499 on a scale where 0.5 is indifference, F(1, 83) = 25.10, p < 0.001, eta-squared 0.232. With 90 participants told only after they had chosen, the reversal held, interval 0.451 to 0.495, F(1, 89) = 20.28, p < 0.001. With 77 told at once and without a delay, nothing happened, interval 0.480 to 0.521, F(1, 76) = 0.005, p = 0.946. Scarpi and Pizzi report the same split in consumer choice: known phantoms are stronger when close and favour the target, unknown phantoms are stronger when far and favour the competitor. Trueblood and Pettibone describe their unknown condition as 60.7% choosing the competitor with the near phantom and 72% with the far one, and those two figures are quoted here from that description rather than from Scarpi and Pizzi. Jarvis and colleagues put an inaccessible preferred food in front of free-ranging swamp wallabies and report that it made the animals switch away from the nutritionally similar food, which they call a net reactance effect.

study.cite: Pettibone, J. C., & Wedell, D. H. (2007). Testing alternative explanations of phantom decoy effects. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 20(3), 323-341.

replicated.unit: difference in the proportion choosing the target

limits: The effect is not spread evenly across people. In Pettibone and Wedell's Experiment 2, 79 of 262 participants showed it clearly, 156 sat in a middle group that produced a significant negative effect for one phantom position, and 27 showed negative effects at all five positions. Need for cognition and choice latency predicted none of that variation. The authors report that the phantom matching the target's better attribute was the position most likely to prompt negative evaluations, and they say the tactic can backfire. Both experiments used undergraduates choosing hypothetical products on two numeric attributes, which is the setting in which the ordinary attraction effect also survives best. No meta-analysis of phantom decoys was located in searches of Crossref, OpenAlex, PubMed and general web search. The 1992 review that names the effect could not be read past its abstract, so the seven generalisations it reports are not stated here. Highhouse's 1996 study of decoy and phantom job candidates is cited throughout this literature, and neither its full text nor an abstract could be retrieved for this entry.
misreadings: A phantom is not the decoy of the pricing-page story. The ordinary decoy sits below the target and can be bought, while the phantom sits above it and cannot. Trueblood and Pettibone separate the two by exactly that, availability to be chosen, and it is the available kind whose robustness the 2014 exceptions concern. Second, the bait and switch reading assumes the shopper hears about the shortage before deciding. Scarpi and Pizzi find that unknown phantoms favour the competitor, and in perceptual choice Trueblood and Pettibone found the competitor favoured whether the withdrawal was announced after a delay or discovered only after the choice. Third, animal work gets quoted as showing the effect is basic rather than cultural. Scarpi's cats moved towards the option similar to the phantom, and only when the phantom was close; the swamp wallabies moved away from it. Fourth, Pratkanis and Farquhar's paper is a review of 13 research literatures, so its seven generalisations are conclusions drawn across other people's studies rather than a result it obtained.

sources.text: Pratkanis, A. R., & Farquhar, P. H. (1992). A brief history of research on phantom alternatives: Evidence for seven empirical generalizations about phantoms. Basic and Applied Social Psychology, 13(1), 103-122. The abstract was read from the record at OpenAlex; the publisher page and the full text could not be retrieved.

Farquhar, P. H., & Pratkanis, A. R. (1993). Decision structuring with phantom alternatives. Management Science, 39(10), 1214-1226. The abstract was read from the record at OpenAlex; the full text could not be retrieved.

Pettibone, J. C., & Wedell, D. H. (2007). Testing alternative explanations of phantom decoy effects. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 20(3), 323-341. Full text read from the author copy hosted by the University of South Carolina. Source for both experiments, the five phantom positions and the individual-difference groups.

Trueblood, J. S., & Pettibone, J. C. (2017). The phantom decoy effect in perceptual decision making. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 30(2), 157-167. Full text read from the author copy hosted by Vanderbilt University; its abstract matches the published abstract at OpenAlex.

Scarpi, D., & Pizzi, G. (2013). The impact of phantom decoys on choices and perceptions. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 26(5), 451-461. The known and unknown phantom result is read from the abstract at OpenAlex; the full text could not be retrieved, and the 60.7% and 72% figures on this page come from Trueblood and Pettibone's description of it.
Scarpi, D. (2011). The impact of phantom decoys on choices in cats. Animal Cognition, 14(1), 127-136. Published online in September 2010. Read from the abstract at PubMed.

Jarvis, G. R., Banks, P. B., Latty, T., Possell, M., Orlando, C. G., & McArthur, C. (2026). A phantom decoy shifts wild forager decisions in a natural environment. Behavioral Ecology, 37(4), arag059. Read from the abstract at the publisher.

Pettibone, J. C., & Wedell, D. H. (2000). Examining models of nondominated decoy effects across judgment and choice. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 81(2), 300-328. Not retrievable; the 57% and 43% figures on this page are quoted from Trueblood and Pettibone's description of it.

Highhouse, S. (1996). Context-dependent selection: The effects of decoy and phantom job candidates. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 65(1), 68-76. Named because this literature cites it as an early phantom study. Neither the full text nor an abstract could be retrieved, and no finding of its is reported here.
